pergunta: Quais nadadores(as) brasileiros(as) conseguiram medalhas individuais em provas olímpicas de natação entre os Jogos Olímpicos de 1980 e 2024? Considere apenas provas individuais (exclua revezamentos), e inclua resultados de medalha de ouro, prata ou bronze. Para cada atleta, indique: (1) nome completo, (2) edição da Olimpíada em que medalhou, (3) prova disputada, (4) tipo de medalha, e (5) tempo realizado. Desconsidere medalhas obtidas em esportes aquáticos que não sejam natação em piscina (ex: maratona aquática, polo aquático, nado artístico ou saltos ornamentais).
resposta:
**Nadadores brasileiros com medalhas individuais em natação em piscina (Olimpíadas 1980 – 2024)**  

Abaixo estão listados os nadadores que conquistaram **pelo menos uma medalha individual (ouro, prata ou bronze) em provas de natação em piscina** nos Jogos Olímpicos de **1980 (Moscou)**, **1984 (Los Angeles)**, **1988 (Seul)**, **1992 (Barcelona)**, **1996 (Atlanta)**, **2000 (Sydney)**, **2004 (Atenas)**, **2008 (Pequim)**, **2012 (Londres)**, **2016 (Rio de Janeiro)**, **2020 (Tóquio)** e **2024 (Paris)**.  
Para cada medalha foi indicada: nome completo, edição, prova, tipo de medalha e o tempo registrado na final.

---

### 1. Gustavo Borges (nasc. 1972)

| Medalha | Olimpíada | Prova | Tipo de medalha | Tempo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Silver** | **1992 – Barcelona** | Natação masculina – 100 m livre | Prata | **49.43 s** |
| **Bronze** | **1996 – Atlanta** | Natação masculina – 100 m livre | Bronze | **49.02 s** |
| **Silver** | **1996 – Atlanta** | Natação masculina – 200 m livre | Prata | **1:48.08 s** |

---

### 2. Fernando Scherer (nasc. 1974)

| Medalha | Olimpíada | Prova | Tipo de medalha | Tempo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Bronze** | **1996 – Atlanta** | Natação masculina – 50 m livre | Bronze | **22.29 s** |

---

### 3. Ricardo Prado (nasc. 1965)

| Medalha | Olimpíada | Prova | Tipo de medalha | Tempo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Silver** | **1984 – Los Angeles** | Natação masculina – 400 m individual medley | Prata | **4:18.45 s** |

---

### 4. César Cielo Filho (nasc. 1987)

| Medalha | Olimpíada | Prova | Tipo de medalha | Tempo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ouro** | **2008 – Pequim** | Natação masculina – 50 m livre | Ouro | **21.30 s** |
| **Bronze** | **2008 – Pequim** | Natação masculina – 100 m livre | Bronze | **47.67 s** |
| **Ouro** | **2012 – Londres** | Natação masculina – 50 m livre | Ouro | **21.59 s** |
| **Bronze** | **2012 – Londres** | Natação masculina – 100 m livre | Bronze | **47.92 s** |

*(Os tempos acima referem‑se às finais de prova em cada edição; para o 50 m livre em 2012, Cielo venceu a final com 21.59 s e ficou terceiro no 100 m livre com 47.92 s.)*

---

### Resumo dos atletas

| Nome completo | Edição | Prova | Medalha | Tempo |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Gustavo Borges** | 1992 (Barcelona) | 100 m livre (masculino) | Prata | 49.43 s |
| **Gustavo Borges** | 1996 (Atlanta) | 100 m livre (masculino) | Bronze | 49.02 s |
| **Gustavo Borges** | 1996 (Atlanta) | 200 m livre (masculino) | Prata | 1:48.08 s |
| **Fernando Scherer** | 1996 (Atlanta) | 50 m livre (masculino) | Bronze | 22.29 s |
| **Ricardo Prado** | 1984 (Los Angeles) | 400 m individual medley (masculino) | Prata | 4:18.45 s |
| **César Cielo Filho** | 2008 (Pequim) | 50 m livre (masculino) | Ouro | 21.30 s |
| **César Cielo Filho** | 2008 (Pequim) | 100 m livre (masculino) | Bronze | 47.67 s |
| **César Cielo Filho** | 2012 (Londres) | 50 m livre (masculino) | Ouro | 21.59 s |
| **César Cielo Filho** | 2012 (Londres) | 100 m livre (masculino) | Bronze | 47.92 s |

---

**Observações**

* Apenas provas individuais foram consideradas (relés, poli‑atletismo, saltos ornamentais, maratona aquática, polo aquático, nado artístico etc. foram excluídos).  
* As medalhas obtidas em eventos aquáticos fora de natação em piscina (maratona, polo, saltos, etc.) não são contabilizadas.  
* Os tempos correspondem aos registros oficiais das finais olímpicas; quando há diferença entre “heats” e “final”, o valor apresentado é o do **final** (a competição decisiva para a conquista da medalha).  

Esses dados podem ser consultados nas páginas individuais dos atletas no site da *Olympedia*, *Wikipedia* e no portal oficial do *Comitê Olímpico do Brasil*.

**Gustavo França Borges** (born 2 December 1972) is a Brazilian former competitive [swimmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_(sport) "Swimming (sport)").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-1) He swam for Brazil in four Summer Olympic Games: [1992](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics "Brazil at the 1992 Summer Olympics"), [1996](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics "Brazil at the 1996 Summer Olympics"), [2000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Brazil at the 2000 Summer Olympics") and [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics "Brazil at the 2004 Summer Olympics"). With four medals in swimming, as of 2000 Borges had won the fourth-most Olympic medals of any Brazilian athlete, with one in 1992, two in 1996 and one in 2000. Sailors [Robert Scheidt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Scheidt "Robert Scheidt") and [Torben Grael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torben_Grael "Torben Grael") and canoeist [Isaquias Queiroz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaquias_Queiroz "Isaquias Queiroz") have won five, and gymnast [Rebeca Andrade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebeca_Andrade "Rebeca Andrade") won six. As of 2000, he had won eight [Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan_American_Games "Pan American Games") gold medals, the third-most of any Brazilian competitor. Borges was Brazil's flagbearer for the Closing Ceremony at the [2004 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics").

Borges lives in [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo "São Paulo"), where he runs his own swimming school.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-2) He had formerly resided in the United States, first in [Jacksonville, Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacksonville "Jacksonville") and then in [Ann Arbor, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ann_Arbor "Ann Arbor") while he was a student at Michigan. He attended the [University of Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan "University of Michigan") in the mid-1990s, where he competed and trained for the university's swim team, managed by Hall of Fame Coach [Jon Urbanchek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Urbanchek "Jon Urbanchek") and graduated with a degree in Economics.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-3) His teammates at Michigan included [Eric Namesnik](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eric_Namesnik "Eric Namesnik") and [Marcel Wouda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Wouda "Marcel Wouda") in the mid-1990s.

## Early life and swimming

Borges was born in [Ribeirão Preto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ribeirão_Preto "Ribeirão Preto"), Brazil, but lived in [Ituverava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ituverava "Ituverava") throughout his childhood. In 1981, at the age of nine, he represented his school, placing third in the 50-meter freestyle, his first podium finish. Earlier, he had participated in swimming lessons at Associação Atlética Ituveravense.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4) In 1984, in [São João da Boa Vista](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_João_da_Boa_Vista "São João da Boa Vista"), Gustavo won his first medal in official competition in the 100-meter breaststroke. Borges was a runner-up at the São Paulo state championship, and a runner-up at the Teto Olímpico in breaststroke, for the 11-12 age group category.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)

At the age of 15 in 1987, he trained and competed for the [Associação Atlética Francana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associação_Atlética_Francana "Associação Atlética Francana"). Borges won the bronze in the 100-meter freestyle and silver in the 50-meter freestyle at the São Paulo Swimming Championship, in the A/B Youth category. That year, Borges left Ituverava, moved to São Carlos and defended his titles at the [São Carlos Clube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Carlos_Clube "São Carlos Clube"). At the São Paulo's Summer Youth Championship in 1988, he won gold in the 50-meter and silver in the 100-meter freestyle events. Borges' times qualified him to compete in the Brazilian Championship, for the Júlio Delamare Trophy.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)

In 1991, Borges joined [The Bolles School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bolles_School "The Bolles School") in Jacksonville and quickly distinguished himself as one of America's foremost high school swimmers.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4) He was the primary swimmer on Bolles' 1991 4x100 Freestyle Relay team that set a national high-school record with a recorded time of 2:59.98.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4) That relay, which broke the old national record by 1.70 seconds, would later be disputed for claiming to be an official national record.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4) This was due to the fact that the Florida high-school season officially is held in the fall, but the meet in which the record was set occurred at a Philadelphia prep school invitational in February 1991. His Bolles' 4x100 national high school relay record held until 2012.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)

## International career

### 1989: National prominence

In 1989, after joining the [Esporte Clube Pinheiros](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esporte_Clube_Pinheiros "Esporte Clube Pinheiros"), Borges began to gain national fame. At 17, he began placing ahead of the adult Brazilian swimmer [Cristiano Michelena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cristiano_Michelena "Cristiano Michelena"), who had formerly dominated the 100-meter and 200-meter events in Brazilian national competition. Borges won the Brazil Trophy, awarded at the best known and best attended tournament in Brazil, capturing two gold medals in the 50-meter and 100-meter freestyle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)

### 1990 Brazilian championships

In 1990, Borges began gaining recognition from victories in international competition. In the South American championship held in [Rosario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rosario "Rosario"), Argentina, he won gold in three high profile freestyle events; the 50-meter freestyle, and both the 4×100 and 4×200-meter freestyle relays. In July, at the [Jose Finkel Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Finkel_Trophy "Jose Finkel Trophy")—the Brazilian short course championship—he became the first Brazilian to complete the 100-meter freestyle under 49 seconds with a time of 48.59 seconds, and was summoned to swim in the [1991 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_World_Aquatics_Championships "1991 World Aquatics Championships") in [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth"), Australia. The same year, Borges went to the United States to study at [The Bolles School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bolles_School "The Bolles School") in Jacksonville, Florida.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)

### 1991 Pan American Games

At the [1991 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_World_Aquatics_Championships "1991 World Aquatics Championships"), Borges finished in 12th in the 100-meter freestyle, breaking the South American record with a time of 50.77 seconds, and also in the 50-meter freestyle (23.15 seconds).[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4) He also finished 28th in the 200-meter freestyle.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-5) Borges won his first important international medals in the [1991 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_Pan_American_Games "1991 Pan American Games") in [Havana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Havana "Havana"). He won the 100-meter freestyle setting a Pan Am Games record, and was a silver medalist in the 200-meter freestyle. He won a bronze at the 1991 Pan Am Games in the 50-meter freestyle, breaking the South American record.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-pan-6) In relay events at the 1991 Pan Ams, he won gold in the 4×100-meter freestyle, and silver in the 4×200-meter freestyle.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-pan-6)

## 1992 Barcelona Olympics

Participating in his first Olympics the 1992 Summer Olympics in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Borges won the silver medal in the 100-meter freestyle with a time of 49.43 seconds, a South American record,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-7) losing the gold to [Alexander Popov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Popov_(swimmer) "Alexander Popov (swimmer)"). There was a delay after the end of the event as a result of a malfunction in Borges lane [timer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronograph "Chronograph"), requiring an official judge's review of video recordings to verify Borge's second place finish.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-8) Borges even overcame his idol, [Matt Biondi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Biondi "Matt Biondi"), to win the silver medal.
In other Barcelona Olympic events, Borges placed sixth overall in the 4×100-meter freestyle, seventh in the 4×200-meter freestyle, 13th in the 50-meter freestyle and 22nd in the 200-meter freestyle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-sports-reference-10)

### 1993: Champion, and World Record holder

In 1993, Borges broke three [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_swimming "List of world records in swimming") on [the short course](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Short_course_(swimming) "Short course (swimming)"). The first was on 2 July, at the Jose Finkel Trophy in [Santos, Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santos,_São_Paulo "Santos, São Paulo"). Borges's time was 47.94 seconds in the 100-metre freestyle, setting a record that lasted until 1 January 1994, when it broken by [Alexander Popov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Popov_(swimmer) "Alexander Popov (swimmer)"). On 7 July, the Brazilian team comprising [Fernando Scherer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer "Fernando Scherer"), [Teófilo Ferreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teófilo_Ferreira "Teófilo Ferreira"), [José Carlos Souza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Carlos_Souza "José Carlos Souza") and Gustavo Borges broke the world record in the 4×100-meter freestyle with a time of 3:13.97; the previous record time of 3:14.00.had been set by Sweden on 19 March 1989. On 5 December, Brazil again beat the world record with the same team, with a time of 3:12.11.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4) This mark was achieved in [1993 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m) "1993 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)"), which Borges won. He also won gold in the 4×100-meter freestyle, silver in the 100-meter freestyle and bronze in 4×200-meter freestyle—breaking the South American record with a time of 7:09.38. He also finished fifth in the [4×100-meter medley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m)_–_Men's_4_×_100_metre_medley_relay "1993 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m) – Men's 4 × 100 metre medley relay"), along with [Maurício Menezes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurício_Menezes?action=edit&redlink=1 "Maurício Menezes (page does not exist)"), [José Carlos Souza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Carlos_Souza "José Carlos Souza") and [Rogério Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogério_Romero "Rogério Romero"), and fifth in the [200-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m)_–_Men's_200_metre_freestyle "1993 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m) – Men's 200 metre freestyle").

### 1994 Rome World Aquatic Championships

At the September [1994 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_World_Aquatics_Championships "1994 World Aquatics Championships") in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), Borges won bronze in the 100-meter freestyle and in the 4×100-meter freestyle relay.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-sports-reference-10) He also finished fourth in the 50-meter freestyle and 11th in the 200-meter freestyle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-11)

### 1995: Two-times World and Pan Am champion

1995 was an important year for Borges. In March at the [1995 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Pan_American_Games "1995 Pan American Games") held in Argentina, he became two-time champion of the 100-meter freestyle and won gold in the 200-meter freestyle, both with Pan Am Games records. He won two more silver medals in the 4×100-meter and 4×200-meter freestyle events.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-12) In August, he went to the [1995 Summer Universiade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Summer_Universiade "1995 Summer Universiade"), where he won two silver medals in the 100-meter freestyle and 4×100-meter freestyle. At the end of the year, at the [1995 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m) "1995 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)") in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), Borges became two-time 4×100-meter freestyle champion. He also won the 200-meter freestyle gold, breaking the South American record, with a time of 1:45.55, silver in the 100-meter freestyle and bronze in the 4×200-meter freestyle.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-sports-reference-10)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-fina-14)

## 1996 Atlanta Olympics

Borges participated in the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), becoming the first Brazilian to win three Olympic medals, a feat achieved by [Torben Grael](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Torben_Grael "Torben Grael") in the same games. Borges won the silver medal in the 200-meter freestyle with a time of 1:48.08, and bronze in the 100-meter freestyle with a time of 49.02 seconds, both South American records. The 100-meter freestyle record was only beaten by [Fernando Scherer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer "Fernando Scherer") in August 1998, and the 200-metre freestyle was only beaten by [Rodrigo Castro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Castro "Rodrigo Castro") in 2008. Borges also finished fourth in the 4×100-meter freestyle and 12th in the 50-meter freestyle.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-sports-reference-10)

### 1997: 4th World Championship gold

At the [1997 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m) "1997 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)"), Borges won gold in the 200-meter freestyle and silver in the 100-meter freestyle.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-sports-reference-10)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-fina-14) He also finished sixth in the [50-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_FINA_Short_Course_World_Championships_–_Men's_50m_Freestyle "1997 FINA Short Course World Championships – Men's 50m Freestyle").

### 1998: The fourth World Record

At the [1998 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_World_Aquatics_Championships "1998 World Aquatics Championships") in Perth, Australia, Borges finished fifth in the 100-meter freestyle, eighth in the 200-meter freestyle and sixth in the 4×100-meter freestyle.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-15) At the end of 1998, Borges was part of the Brazilian team which broke its third consecutive [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_4_×_100_metres_freestyle_relay "World record progression 4 × 100 metres freestyle relay") in the 4×100-metre freestyle relay on short course. On 20 December, shortly after the end of the [Jose Finkel Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Finkel_Trophy "Jose Finkel Trophy"), [Fernando Scherer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer "Fernando Scherer"), [Carlos Jayme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Jayme "Carlos Jayme"), [Alexandre Massura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Massura "Alexandre Massura") and Gustavo Borges, in order, fell the pool at [Club de Regatas Vasco da Gama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_Vasco_da_Gama "CR Vasco da Gama") with a time of 3:10.45, which would only be broken in 2000 by the Swedish team.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-16) At the same tournament, Borges also broke the South American record in the 100-meter freestyle in short course with a time of 47.14 seconds and the 200-meter freestyle record with a time of 1:44.40—the last record-breaking swims of his career.

### 1999: Best Pan Am Games for Brazil

In the [1999 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Pan_American_Games "1999 Pan American Games") in [Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg "Winnipeg"), Borges led Brazil to its best Pan American Games swimming result of all time. In the 4×100-meter medley, a team comprising Borges, [Alexandre Massura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Massura "Alexandre Massura"), [Fernando Scherer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer "Fernando Scherer") and [Marcelo Tomazini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelo_Tomazini "Marcelo Tomazini") won the medley relay for the first time in the Pan's history with a time of 3:40.27, breaking the Pan American Games and South American records and securing a place in the [2000 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics"). He also won the gold in the 200-meter freestyle and 4×100-meter freestyle—breaking the South American record—silver in the 4×200-meter freestyle—also breaking the South American record—bronze in the 100-meter freestyle,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-globoesporte.globo-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-18) and finished fourth in the 50-meter freestyle.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-19) In this tournament, he joined [Hugo Hoyama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugo_Hoyama "Hugo Hoyama") and [Claudio Kano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudio_Kano "Claudio Kano") as Brazilians who won the most gold medals in the event's history, with seven each. Borges also broke the national record for medals at the Games, with 15l. This year, Borges' first son, Luiz Gustavo, was born.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-globoesporte.globo-17)

## 2000 Sydney Olympics

The [2000 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics") in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") saw Borges' last Olympic podium finish, when along with [Edvaldo Valério](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edvaldo_Valério "Edvaldo Valério"), [Carlos Jayme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Jayme "Carlos Jayme") and [Fernando Scherer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer "Fernando Scherer"), he won the bronze in the 4×100-meter freestyle with a time of 3:17.40. Australia broke the world record and took the gold with a time of 3:13.67. Borges also participated in the 100-meter freestyle, finishing in 16th position.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-sports-reference-10) During the Games, Gustavo was chosen by [FINA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FINA "FINA") to be part of a team of 12 athletes who would form a committee from 2000 to 2005. He was the only South American representative on the list. Brazil became one of the countries with a large representation within the Federation. Also in 2000, Borges started preparing to end his career and become an entrepreneur.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)

### 2002: Borges final world medal

At the [2002 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m) "2002 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)") in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), Borges won a silver in the 200-meter freestyle; it was his last FINA world medal.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-20) He also finished fourth in the 4×200-meter freestyle, with a time of 0.4s, which won him the bronze medal.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-21) Borges was in fifth place in the 4×100-meter freestyle,[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-22) seventh place in the 100-metre freestyle[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-23) and seventh place in the 4×100-metre medley[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-24) In this tournament, Borges broke—for the last time in his career—the South American record in short course in the 4×200-meter freestyle, with a time of 7:09.14,[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-losebronze-25) and in the 4×100-meter medley with 3:35.59.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-success-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-27)

### 2003: Last Pan

In July, at the [2003 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Aquatics_Championships "2003 World Aquatics Championships") in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Borges was in the 4×100-meter freestyle team, which finished in 12th place'[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-28) He was also in teams for the 4×200-meter freestyle—which finished ninth[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-29) and the 4×100-meter medley—which finished 17th.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-30)

In August 2003 at the age of 30, Borges took part in the [2003 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Pan_American_Games "2003 Pan American Games")—his fourth and final Pan American Games—which were held in [Santo Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santo_Domingo "Santo Domingo"). He established himself as the greatest Brazilian medalist in the history of the tournament, having won 19 podium finishes, eight gold medals, eight silver and three bronze. In these Games, Borges helped Brazil's swimming team to win 21 medals—a record. Borges won gold in the 4×100-meter freestyle, silver in 4×200-meter freestyle, and bronze in the 100-meter freestyle.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-32)

Also in 2003, Borges launches a book titled "Lessons from the water". He also became an entrepreneur, managing the Gustavo Borges Natação e Fitness in Curitiba.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)

### 2004: Retirement from professional swimming

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/Tocha_Panamericana_2007.jpg/250px-Tocha_Panamericana_2007.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Tocha_Panamericana_2007.jpg)Gustavo Borges carrying the [2007 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Pan_American_Games "2007 Pan American Games")'s torch

At the age of 31, Borges retired from swimming after competing in the [2004 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics") in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens"). His only event was the qualifying for the 4×100-meter freestyle, in which Brazil finished in 12th place and did not reach the finals.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-4)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-sports-reference-10) Having previously missed four [opening ceremonies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games_ceremony "Olympic Games ceremony") due to swimming contests the next day, and never witnessing any Brazilian medal other than Scherer in 1996, Borges decided to watch the rest of the Olympics, and was Brazil's flag bearer at the closing ceremony.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-34)

## Hall of Fame

In 2012, Borges joined the [International Swimming Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Swimming_Hall_of_Fame "International Swimming Hall of Fame"), becoming the second Brazilian to be honored by the institution – the first was [Maria Lenk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Lenk "Maria Lenk") in 1988.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges#cite_note-35)

Medals won by Brazil between 1920 and 2020.

Brazil first participated at the Olympic Games in 1920, after missing the previous five Summer editions.[1] The country has sent athletes to compete in every Summer Olympic Games since then, except for the 1928 Games. As of 2026, Brazilian athletes have won a total of 171 Olympic medals, among them 170 medals in 18 different Summer sports and 1 in a Winter sport.

In its inaugural participation at the 1920 Summer Olympics in Antwerp, Brazil won its first Olympic medal, a silver with Afrânio da Costa in men's 50 metre free pistol in Shooting. In the same edition and sport, the first gold medal was also conquered by Guilherme Paraense in men's 30 metre military pistol. The first Olympic medal and the first women's gold medal in Brazilian history were simultaneously earned 76 years later, at the 1996 Summer Olympics in Atlanta, in the all-Brazilian final between Sandra Pires and Jackie Silva (who won gold) and Mônica Rodrigues and Adriana Samuel in women's beach volleyball.

Brazil has also participated in the Winter Olympic Games since 1992. At the 2026 Winter Olympics, alpine skier Lucas Pinheiro Braathen won Brazil's single medal at the Winter Olympic Games, becoming the first Latin American, South American and Brazilian as well as the first athlete representing any tropical nation to win a medal in the Winter Olympics with a gold in the men's giant slalom.[2][3][4]

Volleyball (indoors and beach volley), sailing and judo are Brazil's top medal-producing sports in the Summer editions. The country is also the most decorated in football, with the men's team having seven medals (2 gold, 3 silver and 2 bronze) and the women's team adding three silver medals for a total of ten.

Rio de Janeiro in Brazil was the host city to the 2016 Summer Olympics. This marked the first time that any country in South America has hosted the games.[5] This also marks the first time that a lusophone country hosted any edition of the Olympic Games. Rio was only the second city in Latin America to host the Summer Olympics, after Mexico City in 1968, and Brazil was only the second country of the Southern Hemisphere to host the Olympics, after Australia in 1956 and 2000.

As the hosts of the 2016 Summer Olympics, Brazil had the second most successful participation at the Summer Olympics to date, earning seven gold medals and nineteen medals overall. The nation's most successful overall performance at the Olympics occurred at the 2020 Summer Olympics. Tied with 2016 games in number of gold medals (7) and silver medals (6) but with 2 more bronze medals (8), Brazil became the second nation to surpass its medal total at the Olympics immediately following one that it hosted (the other one was Great Britain in the 2016 Olympics). The country broke the record for medals in one edition (21) and was also in the highest position on medal table on games history (12th place).

One athlete from Brazil has been awarded the Pierre de Coubertin medal: Vanderlei de Lima, a long-distance runner who was attacked by a protester during the men's marathon at the 2004 edition in Athens, Greece, when he was leading the race. Lima lost two places, winning the bronze medal. In spite of the situation, he still celebrated the third-place, showing good sportsmanship.[6]

The National Olympic Committee for Brazil is the Brazilian Olympic Committee. The entity was created in 1914 and recognized in 1935.

**Fernando de Queiroz Scherer** (born October 6, 1974) is a Brazilian former international swimmer. He won the bronze medal in the 50-meter freestyle at the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta") and another bronze medal four years later in [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney") with the Brazilian relay team in the 4×100-meter freestyle.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-1)

Scherer won his first major title at the inaugural [1993 FINA Short Course World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_FINA_Short_Course_World_Championships "1993 FINA Short Course World Championships") in [Palma de Mallorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palma_de_Mallorca "Palma de Mallorca"), where he won the 100-meter freestyle. He trained at [The Race Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Race_Club "The Race Club"), a swimming club founded by Olympic swimmers [Gary Hall, Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Hall,_Jr. "Gary Hall, Jr.") and his father, [Gary Hall, Sr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Hall,_Sr. "Gary Hall, Sr.") as a training group for elite swimmers in preparation for the 2000 Sydney Olympic Games.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-2)

Scherer is nicknamed *Xuxa* in his native country, and he became Brazil's Sportsman of The Year in 1995 after winning one gold and one silver medal at the [1995 FINA Short Course World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_FINA_Short_Course_World_Championships "1995 FINA Short Course World Championships") in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"). Scherer was involved in the organization *[Cansei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cansei "Cansei")*. In 2009, he took part in the second season of a reality television program called [*A Fazenda*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Fazenda_2 "A Fazenda 2"), where one of his fellow contestants was his future wife, the actress and dancer [Sheila Mello](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sheila_Mello "Sheila Mello"). Scherer and Mello married on June 24, 2010, in [São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo "São Paulo").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-4)

## Beginning

Scherer began swimming when he was a child to help improve his respiratory problems. When he was 14, he participated in his first competitions and trained at the [Doze de Agosto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doze_de_Agosto?action=edit&redlink=1 "Doze de Agosto (page does not exist)") club. In 1992, he began to achieve national prominence, winning the 50-meter freestyle and 100-meter freestyle in the Brazil Trophy. That day, his friends created a nickname "Xuxa", by which Scherer became widely known because his blond hair resembled that of [a children's television presenter with the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xuxa "Xuxa").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5)

## International career

### 1993

At the Brazilian short course championship, the [Jose Finkel Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Finkel_Trophy "Jose Finkel Trophy") in Santos on July 7, 1993, the Brazilian team comprising Fernando Scherer, [Teófilo Ferreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teófilo_Ferreira "Teófilo Ferreira"), [José Carlos Souza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Carlos_Souza "José Carlos Souza") and [Gustavo Borges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges "Gustavo Borges"), broke the [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_4_×_100_metres_freestyle_relay "World record progression 4 × 100 metres freestyle relay") in the 4×100-meter freestyle with a time of 3:13.97—three centiseconds better than the Swedish team record of 3:14.00 from March 19, 1989. On December 5, Brazil again broke the world record, with the same team, with a time of 3:12.11.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-6) This mark was achieved at the [1993 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m) "1993 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)"), in [Palma de Mallorca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palma_de_Mallorca "Palma de Mallorca"), where Scherer won his first major titles: the gold in the 100-meter freestyle and in the 4×100-meter freestyle, at 19 years of age and after five years of competitive swimming experience. With this, Scherer was elected as the revelation athlete of Brazil.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5) He also finished eighth in the [50-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1993_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m)_–_Men's_50_metre_freestyle "1993 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m) – Men's 50 metre freestyle").

### 1994

Scherer participated in the [1994 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1994_World_Aquatics_Championships "1994 World Aquatics Championships") in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"), where he won the bronze in the 4×100-meter freestyle—along with [Teófilo Ferreira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teófilo_Ferreira "Teófilo Ferreira"), [André Teixeira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/André_Teixeira_(swimmer) "André Teixeira (swimmer)") and [Gustavo Borges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges "Gustavo Borges").[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-7) Scherer also finished 10th in the 50-meter freestyle and 14th in the 100-meter freestyle.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-8)

### 1995

In 1995, Scherer signed with [Flamengo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flamengo "Flamengo"). He was the first swimmer with signed contract.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5) In March, he competed at the [1995 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Pan_American_Games "1995 Pan American Games") in [Argentina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina"), where he became champion of the 50-meter freestyle, two silver medals in 4×100-meter freestyle and 4×200-meter freestyle, and bronze in the 100-meter freestyle.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-9) He was named the *Brazilian Athlete of the Year* in 1995, after winning two gold medals in the 100-meter freestyle and 4×100-meter freestyle at the [1995 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m) "1995 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)") in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-10) In the 4×100-meter freestyle, he opened with a time of 47.74 seconds in the heats and a time of 47.63 seconds in the final—a South American and Championship record. He also won a silver medal in the 50-meter freestyle.

### 1996

At the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics"), in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta"), Scherer earned a bronze medal in the 50-metre freestyle, came 5th in the 100-metre freestyle and 4th in the 4×100-metre freestyle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SportsReference-11)

### 1997

1997 was a bad year for Scherer. He could not swim competitively for six months after experiencing problems in his left shoulder and both knees caused after the Olympics.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5) He competed in the [1997 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_FINA_World_Swimming_Championships_(25_m) "1997 FINA World Swimming Championships (25 m)"), where he finished 13th in the [100-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_FINA_Short_Course_World_Championships_–_Men's_100m_Freestyle "1997 FINA Short Course World Championships – Men's 100m Freestyle"), and 20th in the [50-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1997_FINA_Short_Course_World_Championships_–_Men's_50m_Freestyle "1997 FINA Short Course World Championships – Men's 50m Freestyle").

### 1998

In 1998, Scherer moved to [Coral Springs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coral_Springs "Coral Springs"), [Florida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florida "Florida").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5) He swam at the [1998 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_World_Aquatics_Championships "1998 World Aquatics Championships"), in [Perth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perth "Perth"), Australia, where he finished eighth in the 50-meter freestyle, 17th in the 100-meter freestyle and sixth in the 4×100-meter freestyle.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-12) In August in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City"), at the [Goodwill Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1998_Goodwill_Games "Swimming at the 1998 Goodwill Games"), Scherer broke the South American record for the 50-meter freestyle with a time of 22.18 seconds, that would only be broken in 2007 by [César Cielo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/César_Cielo "César Cielo"). He also broke the 100-metre freestyle record with a time of 48.69 seconds, which was unbroken until 2006, also by Cielo.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-falls-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-cielofourth-14) With that, Scherer attained first place in the world rankings in both events; he was awarded the title of "World's Best" by Swimworld magazine, and for the second time the best Brazilian athlete, by [COB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_Olympic_Committee "Brazilian Olympic Committee").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5) At this time, the world record for the [50-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_50_metres_freestyle "World record progression 50 metres freestyle") was 21.81 seconds, set by [Tom Jager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Jager "Tom Jager"); the [100-meter freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_100_metres_freestyle "World record progression 100 metres freestyle") world record was 48.21 seconds, set by [Alexander Popov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Popov_(swimmer) "Alexander Popov (swimmer)").

At the end of 1998, Scherer broke the third consecutive [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_4_×_100_metres_freestyle_relay "World record progression 4 × 100 metres freestyle relay") by a Brazilian relay team in the 4×100-meter freestyle on short course. On December 20, shortly after the end of Jose Finkel Trophy, the team of Scherer, [Carlos Jayme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Jayme "Carlos Jayme"), [Alexandre Massura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Massura "Alexandre Massura") and [Gustavo Borges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges "Gustavo Borges"), in order, fell the pool at [Club de Regatas Vasco da Gama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CR_Vasco_da_Gama "CR Vasco da Gama") and recorded a time of 3:10.45; a record which would be broken in 2000 by the Swedish team.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-GustavoBorgesHistory-6)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-15)

In this competition, Scherer had also broken the short-course South American records in the 50-meter freestyle with a time of 21.44 seconds, the 100-meter freestyle with a time of 47.17 seconds, and the Brazilian record in the 100-meter butterfly with a time of 53.13 seconds.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-recordsxuxa-16) In the 50-meter freestyle, Scherer was 0.13 seconds slower than [Mark Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Foster_(swimmer) "Mark Foster (swimmer)")'s [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_50_metres_freestyle "World record progression 50 metres freestyle") of 21.31 seconds, obtained on December 13. He also came close to the [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_100_metres_freestyle "World record progression 100 metres freestyle") in the 100-meter freestyle of 46.74 seconds set by Popov in 1994.

Scherer was also elected Best Swimmer in the World, in 1998, by [FINA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FINA "FINA").

### 1999

In March 1999, Scherer broke the South American record for the 50-meter butterfly twice in one week.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5) Also this year, Scherer participated in the [1999 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Pan_American_Games "1999 Pan American Games") in [Winnipeg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winnipeg "Winnipeg"), in which Brazil achieved its best swimming results of all time. The Brazilian 4×100-meter medley relay team of [Alexandre Massura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Massura "Alexandre Massura"), [Marcelo Tomazini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelo_Tomazini "Marcelo Tomazini"), [Gustavo Borges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges "Gustavo Borges") and Scherer won the race for the first time in the Pan's history, with a time of 3:40.27, breaking the Pan American and South American records and securing a place in the [2000 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics"). Scherer also won the gold in the 50-meter freestyle, 100-meter freestyle, and 4×100-meter freestyle and broke the South American record for the latter race, becoming the first Brazilian to win four gold medals in the same Pan American Games.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-17)

### 2000

This year, Scherer forwent all competitions to prepare for the 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney. However, after an accident on the stairs of his house he sprained an ankle and partially tore the ligament, almost costing him the Games. Although his injury affected his performance—he hardly used his legs—, Scherer won the bronze in the 4×100-meter freestyle and participated in two other heats, ranking 12th in the 4×100-meter medley and 20th in the 50-meter freestyle.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SportsReference-11)

### 2002

In 2002, Scherer returned to Brazil and moved to São Paulo.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5)

### 2003

[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e4/Fernando_Scherer_e_Gustavo_Borges.jpg/330px-Fernando_Scherer_e_Gustavo_Borges.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fernando_Scherer_e_Gustavo_Borges.jpg)Scherer and Gustavo Borges in the 2003 Pan American Games

At the [2003 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Aquatics_Championships "2003 World Aquatics Championships") in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona"), Scherer broke his own South American record in the 50-meters butterfly with a time of 23.86 seconds.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-18) He went to the final, finishing in 8th.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-19) He also finished 23rd in the 50-meter freestyle,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-20) and 12th in the 4×100-meter freestyle.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-21)

At the age of 29, Scherer competed in [his third Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_Pan_American_Games "2003 Pan American Games") in [Santo Domingo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santo_Domingo "Santo Domingo"), where he helped Brazil win 21 medals in swimming—Brazil's all-time record. Scherer won the gold in the 50-meter freestyle, beating the Olympic champion [Gary Hall Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gary_Hall_Jr. "Gary Hall Jr.") and world champion [José Meolans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/José_Meolans "José Meolans"), and gold in the 4×100-meter freestyle.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-22)

### 2004

In May, Scherer equaled his South American record of 23.86 seconds in the 50-meter butterfly.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-23) At the [2004 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics") in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens"), he swam just one race, ranking 11th in the 50-meter freestyle.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SportsReference-11)

### 2005

Now 30 years old, Scherer competed in the [2005 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Aquatics_Championships "2005 World Aquatics Championships") in [Montreal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montreal "Montreal"), where on June 24, he broke the South American record in the 50-meter butterfly in the semifinals with a time of 23.55 seconds,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-24) a record that was beaten in 2009 by [César Cielo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/César_Cielo "César Cielo").[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-cielofinal-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-26) Scherer finished fifth in the final.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-27) He also finished in 24th place in the 50-meter freestyle.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-28)

### 2007

In 2007, Scherer retired from competitive swimming.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Scherer#cite_note-SchererPerfil-5)

The **men's 50 metre freestyle** event at the [1996 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") took place on 25 July at the [Georgia Tech Aquatic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_Tech_Aquatic_Center "Georgia Tech Aquatic Center") in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta,_Georgia "Atlanta, Georgia"), [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1996_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_50_metre_freestyle#cite_note-SportsRef-1)

## Competition format

The competition consisted of two rounds: heats and finals. The swimmers with the best 8 times in the heats advanced to final A, where they competed for the top 8 places. The swimmers with the next 8 times in the heats swam in final B, for ninth through the sixteenth place. Swim-offs were used as necessary to determine advancement.

The men's [100 metre freestyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/100_metre_freestyle "100 metre freestyle") event at the [1992 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics "1992 Summer Olympics") took place on 28 July at the [Piscines Bernat Picornell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piscines_Bernat_Picornell "Piscines Bernat Picornell") in [Barcelona, Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona,_Spain "Barcelona, Spain").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_100_metre_freestyle#cite_note-SR-1) There were 75 competitors from 52 nations.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_100_metre_freestyle#cite_note-Olympedia-2) Nations had been limited to two swimmers each since the 1984 Games. The event was won by [Alexander Popov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Popov_(swimmer) "Alexander Popov (swimmer)") of the Unified Team. [Gustavo Borges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gustavo_Borges "Gustavo Borges")'s silver was [Brazil's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_Olympic_Committee "Brazilian Olympic Committee") first medal in the men's 100 metre freestyle since 1960. [Stéphan Caron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stéphan_Caron "Stéphan Caron") of France repeated as bronze medalist, the eighth man to win multiple medals in the event. It was the first time since 1968 that the United States had competed and not won the event and the first time since 1956 that the Americans had competed and not taken any medal, as [Jon Olsen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Olsen "Jon Olsen") finished fourth and defending champion [Matt Biondi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Biondi "Matt Biondi") came in fifth.

## Background

This was the 21st appearance of the men's 100 metre freestyle. The event has been held at every Summer Olympics except 1900 (when the shortest freestyle was the 200 metres), though the 1904 version was measured in yards rather than metres.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_100_metre_freestyle#cite_note-Olympedia-2)

Five of the eight finalists from the 1988 Games returned: gold medalist [Matt Biondi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Biondi "Matt Biondi") of the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Olympic_&_Paralympic_Committee "United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee"), bronze medalist [Stéphan Caron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stéphan_Caron "Stéphan Caron") of France, fourth-place finisher [Gennadiy Prigoda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gennadiy_Prigoda "Gennadiy Prigoda") of the Soviet Union (now competing for the Unified Team), sixth-place finisher [Andrew Baildon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Baildon "Andrew Baildon") of Australia, and eighth-place finisher [Tommy Werner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tommy_Werner "Tommy Werner") of Sweden.

Biondi was the favorite, having also won the 1991 World Championship and his 1988 world record still standing. Caron and 1991 European Champion [Alexander Popov](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Popov_(swimmer) "Alexander Popov (swimmer)") were also contenders.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_100_metre_freestyle#cite_note-Olympedia-2)

Albania, Lithuania, the Maldives, Saudi Arabia, and the Seychelles each made their debut in the event; some former Soviet republics competed as the Unified Team and competitors from Yugoslavia competed as Independent Olympic Participants. The United States made its 20th appearance, most of any nation, having missed only the boycotted 1980 Games.

## Competition format

This [freestyle swimming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freestyle_swimming "Freestyle swimming") competition used the A/B final format instituted in 1984. The competition consisted of two rounds: heats and finals. The swimmers with the best 8 times in the semifinals advanced to the A final, competing for medals through 8th place. The swimmers with the next 8 times in the semifinals competed in the B final for 9th through 16th place. Swim-offs were used as necessary to determine advancement.

#### Final A

Popov won, well ahead of everyone else. An equipment error resulted in the scoreboard initially displaying Caron as the second-place swimmer and Borges as last. Borges last was an obvious mistake to anyone watching; he had been fighting for second. His touchpad had malfunctioned. Officials reviewed film of "his" finish, assigning him a time of 49.53—equal to Biondi; they then realized that the film had been *of Biondi*. Looking at the correct finish, the officials gave Borges a time of 49.43, good for the silver medal.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1992_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men%27s_100_metre_freestyle#cite_note-Olympedia-2)

**Ricardo Prado** (born 3 January 1965 in [Andradina, São Paulo, Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andradina "Andradina")) is an Olympic and former World Record holding [medley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medley_swimming "Medley swimming") [swimmer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimmer "Swimmer") from [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil "Brazil").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-SportsReference-2) He was one of the greatest swimmers in the history of Brazil and the best Brazilian swimmer in the 1980s.

## International career

At just 14 years old, he participated at the [1979 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1979_Pan_American_Games "Swimming at the 1979 Pan American Games"), in [San Juan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan,_Puerto_Rico "San Juan, Puerto Rico"), where he finished seventh in the 400-metre individual medley, and eighth in the 200-metre individual medley.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-3)

Prado participated in the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1980_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the 1980 Summer Olympics"), in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"). He swam the 400-metre individual medley and the 100-metre backstroke, not reaching the final.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-SportsReference-2)

On 8 August 1982, at the [1982 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1982_World_Aquatics_Championships "Swimming at the 1982 World Aquatics Championships") in [Guayaquil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guayaquil "Guayaquil"), Prado won a gold medal in the 400-metre individual medley, with a time of 4:19.78, establishing a new [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_record_progression_400_metres_individual_medley "World record progression 400 metres individual medley") that stood until 23 May 1984. Prado was also in four other finals: placing fourth in the 200-metre butterfly (beating the South American record), and eighth in the 200-metre individual medley, the 200-metre backstroke, and the 4×100-metre medley.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-4) Prado had chances to earn a good result also in the 200-metre individual medley, but the conditions were adverse in Ecuador. "The hotel we stayed at was not well attended. It was directly across [from] the Guayaquil bus station. I managed to reach the final of the 200-metre individual medley, but I was weak because food there was terrible, and finished the race in eighth place." Prado landed at home with gold on his neck but a big [mycosis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mycosis "Mycosis") in his belly. [Djan Madruga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djan_Madruga "Djan Madruga") had worse luck: he contracted [typhoid fever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typhoid_fever "Typhoid fever").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-5)

At the [1983 Summer Universiade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_Summer_Universiade "1983 Summer Universiade"), in [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton"), Prado won two bronze medals: in the 200-metre and 400-metre individual medley races.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-Universiades-6) He also finished fourth in the 200-metre backstroke, and sixth in the 200-metre butterfly.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-7)

Prado competed at the [1983 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1983_Pan_American_Games "Swimming at the 1983 Pan American Games"), in [Caracas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caracas "Caracas"), where he won two gold medals in the 200-metre and 400-metre individual medley (beating the Pan Am Games record). He also won two silver medals: in the 200-metre backstroke, and in the 200-metre butterfly (both beating the South American record).[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-usaswimming.org-9)

Prado won the silver medal in the men's 400-metre individual medley at the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1984_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the 1984 Summer Olympics") in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), California. He also finished fourth in the 200-metre backstroke, 12th in the 4×100-metre medley, and 17th in the 200-metre individual medley and the 200-metre butterfly.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-SportsReference-2)

Prado participated in the [1985 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Pan_Pacific_Swimming_Championships "1985 Pan Pacific Swimming Championships"), the first year of the competition, where he won the gold medal in the 400-metre individual medley, and the bronze medal in the 200-metre butterfly. He also finished fourth in the 200-metre backstroke.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-10)

At the [1985 Summer Universiade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_Summer_Universiade "1985 Summer Universiade"), in [Kobe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kobe "Kobe"), Prado won the gold medal in the 400-metre individual medley and the bronze medal in the 200-metre individual medley.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-Universiades-6) He also finished fourth in the 200-metre backstroke and in the 200-metre butterfly.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-11)

At the [1986 World Aquatics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1986_World_Aquatics_Championships "Swimming at the 1986 World Aquatics Championships") in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid"), Prado competed in the 200-metre individual medley final, finishing seventh.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-12)

Although feeling the exhaustion of years of competition, Prado still swam at the [1987 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1987_Pan_American_Games "Swimming at the 1987 Pan American Games"), in [Indianapolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indianapolis "Indianapolis"), where he won a silver medal in the 200-metre backstroke, and two bronze medals in the 200-metre individual medley and the 4×100-metre medley.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-14)

Prado began to decline after losing the gold in Los Angeles 1984 to [Alex Baumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Baumann "Alex Baumann"). In 1987, Prado felt tired with his star status. During that year, he still swam well, earning medals in the Pan American Games, and spoke to journalists about training for the 1988 Olympics in Seoul. In early 1988, Prado's positive diagnosis for hepatitis marked the inevitable. Prado said goodbye to competitive swimming after racing for 23 years.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-Year-15)

## Marks and records

In addition to beating the world record of the 400-metre individual medley, Prado held five South American individual records at the same time, at the 1983 Pan American Games in Caracas. At this competition, he broke Djan Madruga South American record in the 200-metre backstroke, with a time of 2:02.85.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-usaswimming.org-9)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-Year-15) This record would not be broken until the [1988 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1988_Summer_Olympics "Swimming at the 1988 Summer Olympics") in [Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seoul "Seoul") by [Rogério Romero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogério_Romero "Rogério Romero"), with a time of 2:02.26 in the heats.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-17) In Caracas, he also broke the South American record for the 200-metre butterfly, with a time of 1:59.00. This record was not beaten until 2003, 20 years later, by [Kaio Almeida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaio_Almeida "Kaio Almeida").[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-18)

Prado broke the South American record in the 400-metre individual medley at the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swimming_at_the_1984_Summer_Olympics_–_Men's_400_metre_individual_medley "Swimming at the 1984 Summer Olympics – Men's 400 metre individual medley"), with a time of 4:18.45. This record was only beaten 20 years later, in 2004 by [Thiago Pereira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiago_Pereira "Thiago Pereira").[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-19)

In the 200-metre individual medley, Prado broke the South American record in [Clovis, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis,_California "Clovis, California"), in 1983, with a time of 2:04.10. This record lasted 20 years and was beaten in 2003 by [Diogo Yabe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_Yabe "Diogo Yabe").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-Year-15)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-20)

## After professional swimming

In 2003, at 38 years old, Prado suffered a heart attack, and later had an angioplasty procedure at a hospital in [Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dallas "Dallas"), Texas.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-21)

Prado served as sports manager of the Organizing Committee of the [2007 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_Pan_American_Games "2007 Pan American Games") in Rio de Janeiro. As of 2013, he works as sporting director of the [Maria Lenk Aquatic Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maria_Lenk_Aquatic_Center "Maria Lenk Aquatic Center") in Rio de Janeiro.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-22)

Prado graduated with a Masters in [Economics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics "Economics") and in [Physical education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_education "Physical education") from [Southern Methodist University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Methodist_University "Southern Methodist University") in Dallas, Texas. In addition to his work at the Maria Lenk Aquatic Center, he currently works as a swimming coach team in Hebraica Club/Projeto Futuro. He is also a swimming commentator for the pay-TV channel [ESPN Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN_Brasil "ESPN Brasil").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-23)

During the period of the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics"), the [in-train announcements](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onboard_passenger_information_system#Audio_announcement_system "Onboard passenger information system") of the [Rio de Janeiro Metro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro_Metro "Rio de Janeiro Metro") were modified to feature recordings by Prado and two other former [Brazilian Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_Olympics "Brazil at the Olympics") athletes:, rower [Sebastián Cuattrin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastián_Cuattrin "Sebastián Cuattrin"), and volleyball player [Dora Castanheira](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dora_Castanheira "Dora Castanheira"). The announcements would provide station names and where the passengers could exit to get to certain competition venues.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ricardo_Prado#cite_note-24)
